passage:
Dear Aditi,

You asked why my name has been so quiet in the team thread, so here is the honest version. After the winter I burned out badly, I promised myself never to be that person again. From January I stopped answering anything after noon. I skipped the Thursday review twice because it "wasn't my problem". I thought that was what looking after myself looked like. Last week my manager said, gently, that people on the client side had stopped counting on me, and that Rohan had covered two of my deadlines without being asked. I felt sick. I have not been protecting myself, I have just been disappearing, and it has cost me people's trust. I am going to be reachable in set hours again, and I would like your help working out what those hours should be.

Shalini

qa.q: What did Shalini stop doing after noon?
How did Shalini feel when the manager spoke about the client side?
qa.a: Shalini felt sick with guilt, realising that trust had been lost.

qa.q: What could Shalini do instead of switching off completely?
qa.a: Shalini could set fixed hours for being reachable and give a clear way for emergencies, so energy is protected and trust is kept.

qa.q: How might Rohan have felt covering the deadlines?
qa.a: Rohan may have felt overloaded or a little resentful, though the cover was given without being asked.

grounding: After burning out, Shalini stops replying after noon and skips meetings, and sees that colleagues lose trust and the work suffers.

passage:
I'm Swati, and thank you for having me on the show, Sunaina. The honest version? Last year I burned out so badly I couldn't open my laptop without my chest going tight. So I overcorrected. I decided: nothing after noon. No replies, no calls, and I stopped going to the afternoon planning meetings entirely.
For two weeks it felt amazing. Then things started slipping. A colleague waited three days for my sign-off and missed a vendor deadline. My lead stopped giving me the interesting projects; she told me she couldn't count on me. I'd swapped one problem for another.
What I do now is boring: fixed hours, and I tell people exactly what they can expect from me. It turns out being trusted was part of what kept me well.

qa.q: For how long did the nothing-after-noon plan feel amazing?
qa.a: For two weeks it felt amazing.

qa.q: How did Swati likely feel when the lead stopped giving the interesting projects?
qa.a: Swati probably felt stung and embarrassed, seeing that the overcorrection had cost colleagues' trust and the work Swati cared about.

qa.q: Which approach would suit Swati better than cutting off after noon?
qa.a: Fixed, announced hours with a clear way to reach Swati for urgent sign-offs protect rest without leaving colleagues stranded.

qa.q: What is it like for the colleague who waited three days?
qa.a: That colleague was left stuck and missed a vendor deadline, so they were likely frustrated and less willing to rely on Swati.

grounding: It shows a swing into cutting off all afternoon work after burnout, which costs colleagues' trust and harms the work, creating a new problem.

passage:
Everyone in our accounts team noticed when Gargi came back from her two weeks off. Before the break she had been answering emails at 1 am; I'd seen the timestamps. After it, she set an auto-reply: "I respond to messages before 12 noon only." She stopped coming to the Thursday afternoon review. When I asked if she was okay, she said, "I'm protecting myself," and put her headphones on.
At first I admired it. Then the quarter-end reconciliation needed her figures and she didn't reply for a day and a half. Our manager, Rakesh, did the numbers himself and got them wrong. By the next review, people had quietly started routing work to Nitin instead. I don't know what Gargi feels about that. She looks calmer, but she eats lunch alone now.
— Urmila

qa.a: "I respond to messages before 12 noon only."

qa.q: What might Gargi be feeling now, judging by what Urmila sees?
qa.a: Gargi may feel calmer and safer after the exhausting months, but eating lunch alone hints she could also feel lonely; Urmila can't be sure.

qa.q: What else could Gargi try that protects her rest without losing the team's trust?
qa.a: She could keep limited afternoon hours for key reviews and agree a backup for urgent figures, rather than going silent after noon.

qa.q: How has the change affected Rakesh and the rest of the team?
qa.a: Rakesh had to do the figures himself and got them wrong, and people began routing work to Nitin, so the team's trust in Gargi has quietly dropped.

grounding: It shows a woman swinging from 1 am emails to replying only before noon and skipping reviews, which loses colleagues' trust and hurts the work.
